questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Quadratic Equation Given an Imaginary Root and Its Leading Coefficient
questions.problem: A quadratic equation in the variable $x$ with real coefficients has a root $x=-\,\frac{6\text{i}}{\sqrt{5}}.$ Given that the coefficient of ${x}^{2}$ in the equation is $5,$ find the equation.
questions.worked_solution:
Since the quadratic equation has real coefficients and  $x=-\,\frac{6\text{i}}{\sqrt{5}}$ is a root, its conjugate  $x=\frac{6\text{i}}{\sqrt{5}}$ must also be a root. Therefore, using the zero product property, we can write a quadratic equation with the required roots as follows:

$$
(x-\frac{6\text{i}}{\sqrt{5}})(x+\frac{6\text{i}}{\sqrt{5}})=0
$$

Multiplying out the parentheses and simplifying gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-{(\frac{6\text{i}}{\sqrt{5}})}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-\frac{36}{5}(-1) & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+\frac{36}{5} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation has roots $x=\pm \frac{6\text{i}}{\sqrt{5}},$ but the coefficient of ${x}^{2}$ is not $5.$ Therefore, to find the desired equation, we multiply the equation above by $5.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}5({x}^{2}+\frac{36}{5}) & =0 \\ 5{x}^{2}+36 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A quadratic equation in the variable $x$ with real coefficients has a root $x=-3\text{i}.$ Given that the coefficient of ${x}^{2}$ in the equation is $-5$, find the equation.
questions.worked_solution:
Since the quadratic equation has real coefficients and  $x=-3\text{i}$ is a root, its conjugate  $x=3\text{i}$ must also be a root. Therefore, using the zero product property, we can write a quadratic equation with the required roots as follows:

$$
(x-3\text{i})(x+3\text{i})=0
$$

Multiplying out the parentheses and simplifying gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-(3\text{i})^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-9(-1) & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+9 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation has roots $x=\pm 3\text{i},$ but the coefficient of ${x}^{2}$ is not $-5.$ Therefore, to find the desired equation, we multiply the equation above by $-5.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-5({x}^{2}+9) & =0 \\ -5{x}^{2}-45 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: A quadratic equation in the variable $x$ with real coefficients has a root $x=-\text{i}.$ Given that the coefficient of ${x}^{2}$ in the equation is $-2$, find the equation.
questions.worked_solution:
Since the quadratic equation has real coefficients and  $x=-\text{i}$ is a root, its conjugate  $x=\text{i}$ must also be a root. Therefore, using the zero product property, we can write a quadratic equation with the required roots as follows:

$$
(x-\text{i})(x+\text{i})=0
$$

Multiplying out the parentheses and simplifying gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-(\text{i})^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-(-1) & =0 \\ {x}^{2}+1 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

This equation has roots $x=\pm \text{i},$ but the coefficient of ${x}^{2}$ is not $-2.$ Therefore, to find the desired equation, we multiply the equation above by $-2.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-2({x}^{2}+1) & =0 \\ -2{x}^{2}-2 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding a Quadratic Equation Given a Complex Root and Its Leading Coefficient
questions.problem:
A quadratic equation with real coefficients has a complex root $x=\sqrt{2}+3\text{i}.$ Given that the coefficient of ${x}^{2}$ in the equation is $1,$ find the equation. Write your answer in the form $a{x}^{2}+bx+c=0,$ where $a,$ $b,$ and $c$ are real constants.

{{field-1}}$=0$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the quadratic equation has real coefficients and $x=\sqrt{2}+3\text{i}$ is a root, we know that its complex conjugate $x=\sqrt{2}-3\text{i}$ is also a root. Therefore, using the zero product property, we can write a quadratic equation with the required roots as follows:

$$
(x-(\sqrt{2}+3\text{i}))(x-(\sqrt{2}-3\text{i}))=0
$$

By expanding the parentheses, we can write the equation in standard form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-x(\sqrt{2}+3\text{i})-x(\sqrt{2}-3\text{i})+(\sqrt{2}+3\text{i})(\sqrt{2}-3\text{i}) & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-\sqrt{2}x-\cancel{3x\text{i}}-\sqrt{2}x+\cancel{3x\text{i}}+2-9{\text{i}}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-2\sqrt{2}\,x+2+9 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-2\sqrt{2}\,x+11 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
A quadratic equation in the variable $x$ with real coefficients has a root $x=2+\sqrt{3}\,\text{i}.$ Given that the coefficient of ${x}^{2}$ in the equation is $5,$ find the equation. Write your answer in the form $a{x}^{2}+bx+c=0,$ where $a,$ $b,$ and $c$ are real constants.

{{field-1}}$=0$
questions.worked_solution:
Since the quadratic equation has real coefficients and $x=2+\sqrt{3}\,\text{i}$ is a root, its conjugate $x=2-\sqrt{3}\,\text{i}$ must also be a root. Therefore, using the zero product property, we can write a quadratic equation with the required roots as follows:

$$
(x-(2+\sqrt{3}\,\text{i}))(x-(2-\sqrt{3}\,\text{i}))=0
$$

By expanding the parentheses, we can write the equation in standard form as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}-x(2+\sqrt{3}\,\text{i})-x(2-\sqrt{3}\,\text{i})+(2+\sqrt{3}\,\text{i})(2-\sqrt{3}\,\text{i}) & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-2x-\cancel{x\sqrt{3}\,\text{i}}-2x+\cancel{x\sqrt{3}\,\text{i}}+4-3{\text{i}}^{2} & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-4x+4+3 & =0 \\ {x}^{2}-4x+7 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

This equation has roots $x=2\pm \sqrt{3}\,\text{i},$ but the coefficient of ${x}^{2}$ is not $5.$ Therefore, to find the desired equation, we multiply the equation above by $5.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}5({x}^{2}-4x+7) & =0 \\ 5{x}^{2}-20x+35 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$
